drills.title: It's or Its?
drills.blurb: The apostrophe test that trips up everyone.

items.prompt: The dog wagged ___ tail happily.
items.explain: "Its" is possessive (no apostrophe); "it's" only ever means "it is" or "it has".

items.prompt: ___ raining again this afternoon.
items.explain: "It's" = "it is" — test it: "It is raining" works, so the apostrophe belongs.

items.prompt: The robot lost ___ balance on the stairs.
items.explain: The balance belongs to the robot, so use possessive "its" — no apostrophe, just like "his" and "hers".

items.prompt: I think ___ time for lunch.
items.explain: "It is time for lunch" makes sense, so contract it to "it's" with the apostrophe.

items.prompt: The team celebrated ___ first win of the season.
items.explain: The win belongs to the team — possessive "its" never takes an apostrophe.

items.prompt: ___ been a long day at the museum.
items.explain: "It's" can also mean "it has" — "It has been a long day" expands correctly.

items.prompt: The comet returns when ___ orbit brings it close.
items.explain: The orbit belongs to the comet — "it is orbit" fails the swap test, so it's possessive "its".

items.prompt: Every country protects ___ own borders.
items.explain: Possession again: like "his own" or "her own," write "its own" with no apostrophe.

items.prompt: ___ a shame the game was rained out.
items.explain: "It is a shame" works when expanded, so the contraction "it's" is correct.

items.prompt: The volcano showed signs that ___ about to erupt.
items.explain: Expand it: "it is about to erupt" — a working "it is" means apostrophe.

items.prompt: The committee gave ___ final approval yesterday.
items.explain: Possessive "its" has no apostrophe anywhere — "its'" is never a real word.

items.prompt: I wonder if ___ going to snow tonight.
items.explain: "It is going to snow" expands cleanly, so use "it's" — and "its'" doesn't exist.

items.prompt: ___ taken the crew months to repair the bridge.
items.explain: Here "it's" = "it has" — "It has taken months" works, and only the contraction gets an apostrophe.

items.prompt: The snail carries ___ shell wherever it goes.
items.explain: The shell belongs to the snail — possessive "its" takes no apostrophe, just like "his".

items.prompt: ___ almost midnight, so let's head home.
items.explain: "It is almost midnight" expands cleanly, so the contraction "it's" gets the apostrophe.

items.prompt: The library extended ___ weekend hours.
items.explain: The hours belong to the library — "it is weekend hours" fails the swap test, so use possessive "its".

items.prompt: Careful — ___ scorching hot in the attic.
items.explain: "It is scorching hot" works when expanded, so the apostrophe belongs.

items.prompt: The kitten chased ___ own shadow across the porch.
items.explain: The shadow belongs to the kitten — like "his own," write "its own" with no apostrophe.

items.prompt: ___ been years since the theater sold out a show.
items.explain: "It's" can mean "it has" — "It has been years" expands correctly, so keep the apostrophe.

items.prompt: The glacier is losing ___ ice faster every decade.
items.explain: The ice belongs to the glacier — possession means "its," no apostrophe.

items.prompt: Tell me when ___ safe to cross the street.
items.explain: "When it is safe" expands cleanly, so the contraction "it's" is correct.

items.prompt: The company doubled ___ profits after the merger.
items.explain: The profits belong to the company — "it is profits" fails, so it's possessive "its".

items.prompt: ___ hard to believe summer is already over.
items.explain: "It is hard to believe" works, so contract it to "it's" with the apostrophe.

items.prompt: The novel is famous for ___ surprise twist ending.
items.explain: The ending belongs to the novel — ownership takes apostrophe-free "its".

items.prompt: Grab a jacket — ___ been freezing all morning.
items.explain: "It has been freezing" expands correctly, so use "it's" — and "its'" is never a real word.

items.prompt: The orchestra tuned ___ instruments before the overture.
items.explain: The instruments belong to the orchestra — possessive "its" never takes an apostrophe, anywhere.

items.prompt: Do you really think ___ worth waiting in that line?
items.explain: "It is worth waiting" expands cleanly, so choose "it's" — "its'" doesn't exist.

items.prompt: The startup owes ___ rapid success to word of mouth.
items.explain: The success belongs to the startup — "it is rapid success" fails, so possessive "its" wins.

items.prompt: ___ going to love this recipe.
items.explain: "You're" = "you are"; "your" shows possession. Expand it: "You are going…" works.

items.prompt: Don't forget ___ umbrella today.
items.explain: The umbrella belongs to you, so use possessive "your" — "you are umbrella" makes no sense.

items.prompt: ___ homework is on the kitchen table.
items.explain: Possession: the homework is yours, so "your" — the apostrophe version only means "you are".

items.prompt: I heard ___ moving to Denver next month.
items.explain: "I heard you are moving" expands perfectly, so the contraction "you're" is right.

items.prompt: Is this ___ backpack?
items.explain: The backpack belongs to you — possessive "your," since "Is this you are backpack?" fails.

items.prompt: Call me when ___ finished with practice.
items.explain: "When you are finished" works, so contract it to "you're" with the apostrophe.

items.prompt: ___ welcome to join us for dinner.
items.explain: "You are welcome" expands correctly — "you're welcome" always takes the apostrophe.

items.prompt: The coach praised ___ effort in the final lap.
items.explain: The effort is yours — possessive "your," because "praised you are effort" makes no sense.

items.prompt: ___ sure this shortcut leads to the trail?
items.explain: It's really "Are you sure…?" flipped — "You are sure?" works, so use "you're".

items.prompt: Raise ___ hand if you know the answer.
items.explain: The hand belongs to you — possessive "your" never gets an apostrophe.

items.prompt: ___ being too hard on yourself.
items.explain: "You are being too hard" expands cleanly — the "are" test always settles it.

items.prompt: I can tell ___ favorite planet is Saturn.
items.explain: The favorite planet belongs to you — "you are favorite planet" fails, so it's possessive "your".

items.prompt: ___ the only one who read the whole chapter.
items.explain: "You are the only one" works when expanded, so the apostrophe version wins.

items.prompt: Wipe ___ feet before coming inside.
items.explain: The feet belong to you — possessive "your," since "wipe you are feet" makes no sense.

items.prompt: ___ late for the bus again!
items.explain: "You are late" expands perfectly, so the contraction "you're" is right.

items.prompt: Hand the usher ___ ticket at the gate.
items.explain: The ticket belongs to you — possession means "your," no apostrophe.

items.prompt: I hope ___ feeling better today.
items.explain: "I hope you are feeling better" works, so use the contraction "you're".

items.prompt: ___ bike has a flat tire.
items.explain: The bike belongs to you — "You are bike" fails the swap test, so it's possessive "your".

items.prompt: Text me once ___ on the train.
items.explain: "Once you are on the train" expands cleanly — a working "you are" means apostrophe.

items.prompt: The judges were amazed by ___ card trick.
items.explain: The trick belongs to you — "amazed by you are card trick" fails, so possessive "your".

items.prompt: ___ not going to believe who won the raffle.
items.explain: "You are not going to believe" works when expanded, so "you're" is correct.

items.prompt: Keep ___ voice down during the movie.
items.explain: The voice is yours — possessive "your" never takes an apostrophe.

items.prompt: If ___ hungry, there's soup on the stove.
items.explain: "If you are hungry" expands correctly, so contract it to "you're".

items.prompt: The dentist said ___ next checkup is in June.
items.explain: The checkup belongs to you — "you are next checkup" fails, so it's possessive "your".

items.prompt: I can't understand you when ___ mumbling.
items.explain: "When you are mumbling" works — before an -ing action like this, the "are" test says "you're".

items.prompt: Whatever ___ decision is, we'll support it.
items.explain: The decision belongs to you — "whatever you are decision" fails, so possessive "your" wins.

items.prompt: No matter ___ age, the trail is worth hiking.
items.explain: The age is yours — "no matter you are age" makes no sense, so use possessive "your".

items.prompt: ___ about to see something incredible.
items.explain: "You are about to see" expands cleanly — the "are" test settles it.

items.prompt: Put the groceries over ___ by the door.
items.explain: "There" points to a place — it has "here" hiding inside it.

items.prompt: The students finished ___ science projects early.
items.explain: The projects belong to the students — possessive "their" has "heir" inside, and heirs own things.

items.prompt: ___ coming to the game tonight.
items.explain: "They are coming" expands perfectly, so use the contraction "they're".

items.prompt: ___ are three eggs left in the carton.
items.explain: "There are" states that something exists — no ownership, no "they are".

items.prompt: The birds built ___ nest in the oak tree.
items.explain: The nest belongs to the birds — possessive "their," since "they are nest" fails.

items.prompt: I think ___ hiding the presents in the garage.
items.explain: "They are hiding" works when expanded, so the contraction "they're" is correct.

items.prompt: We hiked to the summit and camped ___.
items.explain: It names the place we camped — "there" contains "here," your clue for locations.

items.prompt: The Vikings named ___ ships after sea creatures.
items.explain: The ships belonged to the Vikings — ownership means "their".

items.prompt: ___ the fastest relay team in the district.
items.explain: "They are the fastest team" expands cleanly, so it's "they're".

items.prompt: ___ is no shortcut to mastering the piano.
items.explain: "There is" announces existence — nothing is owned and no one "is" anything.

items.prompt: Ask the neighbors if ___ dog can play outside.
items.explain: The dog belongs to the neighbors — "they are dog" fails, so possessive "their" wins.

items.prompt: The twins say ___ allergic to peanuts, not tree nuts.
items.explain: "They are allergic" works when expanded — the apostrophe marks the missing "a" in "are".

items.prompt: Scientists believe ___ may be water on Europa.
items.explain: "There may be" states existence, like "there is" — no possession, no "they are".

items.prompt: The chess players shook hands before ___ match.
items.explain: The match belongs to the players — possessive "their" has "heir" inside, and heirs own things.

items.prompt: ___ practicing for the talent show upstairs.
items.explain: "They are practicing" expands perfectly, so use the contraction "they're".

items.prompt: Sign your name ___ at the bottom of the page.
items.explain: It points to a spot on the page — "there" has "here" hiding inside, your clue for places.

items.prompt: The ants carried crumbs back to ___ colony.
items.explain: The colony belongs to the ants — "they are colony" fails, so possessive "their" wins.

items.prompt: ___ selling lemonade on the corner today.
items.explain: "They are selling lemonade" works when expanded, so it's "they're".

items.prompt: ___ used to be a train station on this street.
items.explain: "There used to be" states that something existed, like "there is" — no ownership, no "they are".

items.prompt: The astronauts checked ___ suits before the spacewalk.
items.explain: The suits belong to the astronauts — ownership means "their".

items.prompt: Call the plumbers and ask when ___ available.
items.explain: "When they are available" expands cleanly, so the contraction "they're" is correct.

items.prompt: ___ wasn't a single cloud in the sky.
items.explain: "There wasn't" states existence (or the lack of it) — nothing is owned and no one "is" anything.

items.prompt: The dancers took ___ places as the curtain rose.
items.explain: The places belong to the dancers — "they are places" fails, so possessive "their" wins.

items.prompt: I doubt ___ open on Thanksgiving.
items.explain: "I doubt they are open" expands correctly — the apostrophe marks the missing "a" in "are".

items.prompt: If ___ ever was a time to speak up, it's now.
items.explain: "There ever was" announces existence, like "there is" — no possession and no "they are".

items.prompt: The owls hunt at dusk because ___ prey wakes up then.
items.explain: The prey belongs to the owls — "they are prey" fails the swap test, so it's possessive "their".

items.prompt: The referees admitted ___ still reviewing the play.
items.explain: "They are still reviewing" works when expanded, so use the contraction "they're".

items.prompt: The map claims ___ is buried treasure on the island.
items.explain: "There is buried treasure" states existence — the place-and-existence word with "here" inside.

items.prompt: Cheetahs run faster ___ any other land animal.
items.explain: "Than" compares; "then" tells time — both the comparison word and "than" have an A.

items.prompt: We ate dinner, and ___ we watched a movie.
items.explain: "Then" marks what happens next in time — "then" and "time" share an E-for-events feel, while "than" only compares.

items.prompt: My backpack is heavier ___ yours.
items.explain: Heavier is a comparison, and comparisons take "than" — the one with an A.

items.prompt: First stretch, ___ start your run.
items.explain: It's a sequence in time — first this, "then" that.

items.prompt: Mount Everest is taller ___ K2.
items.explain: Taller sets up a comparison, so it's "than" — comparison and "than" both carry an A.

items.prompt: If it rains, ___ the picnic moves indoors.
items.explain: "If…then" shows consequence — "then" handles time, sequence, and results.

items.prompt: He'd rather read ___ scroll on his phone.
items.explain: "Rather…than" is a fixed comparing pair — preferring one thing over another always takes "than".

items.prompt: Gas cost far less back ___.
items.explain: "Back then" points to a past time, and time words take "then" with an E.

items.prompt: The experiment took longer ___ we expected.
items.explain: Longer compares the real time to the expected time, so use comparing "than".

items.prompt: Finish your homework; ___ you may play outside.
items.explain: One event follows another — sequence means "then," the time word.

items.prompt: No sooner had we sat down ___ the phone rang.
items.explain: "No sooner…than" is a comparison of timing — the "sooner" (a comparative) locks in "than".

items.prompt: I'd sooner walk ___ pay for parking.
items.explain: "Sooner…than" compares two choices — any comparative like "sooner" demands "than".

items.prompt: Every now and ___, the lighthouse light flickers.
items.explain: "Every now and then" is a set time expression — moments in time always take "then".

items.prompt: The lake is deeper ___ it looks from the shore.
items.explain: "Deeper" is a comparative, and comparatives always take "than" — the compArison word with an A.

items.prompt: Mix the flour and eggs; ___ fold in the blueberries.
items.explain: One step follows another in time, so use "then" — the sEquence word with an E.

items.prompt: Nothing smells better ___ fresh bread in the oven.
items.explain: "Better" sets up a comparison, and every comparison takes "than" with an A.

items.prompt: We'll tour the aquarium first and eat lunch ___.
items.explain: It means "at that time, afterward" — a time word, so "then" with an E.

items.prompt: Other ___ a few typos, the essay was flawless.
items.explain: "Other than" is a fixed pair meaning "except for" — it's always "than," never "then."

items.prompt: If the fire alarm sounds, ___ everyone exits through the gym.
items.explain: "If…then" states a consequence — results and sequences belong to "then."

items.prompt: He would rather repair the old bike ___ buy a new one.
items.explain: "Rather…than" weighs two choices against each other — preference is a comparison, so "than."

items.prompt: Phones were rare back ___, so most families shared one line.
items.explain: "Back then" points to a past time — time expressions always take "then" with an E.

items.prompt: The repair cost less ___ fifty dollars.
items.explain: "Less than" compares an amount to a limit — any comparative like "less" demands "than."

items.prompt: By ___, the ferry had already left the dock.
items.explain: "By then" means "by that time" — a moment in time, so it's "then."

items.prompt: No sooner had the curtain risen ___ the stage lights failed.
items.explain: "No sooner…than" compares two timings — the comparative "sooner" locks in "than," even though it feels like a time word.

items.prompt: Just ___, a knock at the door interrupted the meeting.
items.explain: "Just then" means "at that exact moment" — a point in time, so "then" with an E.

items.prompt: No one knows this coastline better ___ the old lighthouse keeper.
items.explain: "Better" compares the keeper's knowledge to everyone else's — comparisons take "than," even at the end of a sentence.

items.prompt: Knead the dough thoroughly, and only ___ let it rise.
items.explain: "Only then" means "only at that point" — it orders steps in time, so "then."

items.prompt: If practice matters more ___ talent, then effort decides everything.
items.explain: Don't let the later "then" fool you — "more" sets up a comparison, and comparisons take "than."

drills.title: Affect or Effect?
drills.blurb: Usually a verb versus a noun.

items.prompt: Loud music can ___ your concentration.
items.explain: "Affect" is the verb (to influence); "effect" is the noun (the result). A = Action.

items.prompt: The new law had little ___ on traffic.
items.explain: After "had little," you need the noun "effect" — the End result starts with E.

items.prompt: Cold weather can ___ your mood.
items.explain: You need an action word here, so use the verb "affect" — A = Action.

items.prompt: Drowsiness is a common side ___ of this medicine.
items.explain: "Side effect" is always the noun "effect" — the result the medicine causes.

items.prompt: Did the rain ___ your weekend plans?
items.explain: The rain performs an action on your plans, so use the verb "affect."

items.prompt: Skipping breakfast can ___ your focus at school.
items.explain: After "can" you need a verb, and the verb of influence is "affect."

items.prompt: The special ___ in that movie were stunning.
items.explain: Movies have "special effects" — a noun naming the results on screen.

items.prompt: One kind word can have a big ___.
items.explain: After "a big" you need a noun, so it's "effect" — E = End result.

items.prompt: How does sleep ___ memory?
items.explain: "Does" signals a verb is coming, and the verb is "affect" (to influence).

items.prompt: The volcano's ash had a lasting ___ on the climate.
items.explain: "A lasting ___" needs a noun, so choose "effect," the result.

items.prompt: His speech had a powerful ___ on the voters.
items.explain: The article "a" points to a noun, and the noun for a result is "effect."

items.prompt: Even small habits can deeply ___ your health.
items.explain: You can swap in "influence" here, so it's the verb "affect" — A = Action.

items.prompt: The experiment produced a surprising ___ in the plants.
items.explain: What was produced is a thing (a result), so use the noun "effect."

items.prompt: The ___ of the caffeine wore off by noon.
items.explain: "The ___ of" calls for a noun, and the noun for a result is "effect" — E = End result.

items.prompt: One rainy day won't ___ the harvest.
items.explain: After "won't" you need a verb, and the verb of influence is "affect" — A = Action.

items.prompt: Today's science lesson covered cause and ___.
items.explain: The pair is "cause and effect" — a cause is a thing and so is its result, the noun "effect."

items.prompt: Pollution can greatly ___ river wildlife.
items.explain: "Greatly ___" describes an action being done to the wildlife, so use the verb "affect."

items.prompt: The haunted house used spooky sound ___ to scare visitors.
items.explain: "Sound effects" are things you can list — nouns — so it's "effects" with an E.

items.prompt: The referee's call didn't ___ the final score.
items.explain: Swap in "influence": "didn't influence the score" works, so it's the verb "affect."

items.prompt: Scientists measured the ___ of fertilizer on corn growth.
items.explain: You measure a thing, not an action — "the ___ of" always takes the noun "effect."

items.prompt: Will the road closure ___ your commute tomorrow?
items.explain: "Will" signals a verb is coming, and the verb of influence is "affect" — A = Action.

items.prompt: The only side ___ was a mild headache.
items.explain: A "side effect" is a result you can name — a noun — so it's always "effect."

items.prompt: Gravity ___ everything that has mass.
items.explain: Gravity is doing something to everything — an action — so use the verb "affects."

items.prompt: The new curfew took ___ at midnight.
items.explain: "Take effect" is a set phrase — the law starts working, and what it takes is the noun "effect."

items.prompt: Rising interest rates ___ buyers and renters alike.
items.explain: The rates are acting on people — swap in "influence" and it works, so it's the verb "affect."

items.prompt: One factory closing triggered a domino ___ across the region.
items.explain: "A domino ___" needs a noun after the article "a" — the chain result is the noun "effect."

items.prompt: The lawyers debated whether the ruling would ___ earlier contracts.
items.explain: After "would" comes a verb, and the verb meaning "to influence" is "affect" — A = Action.

items.prompt: His apology had the opposite ___ and made things worse.
items.explain: "The opposite ___" names a thing that happened — a result — so it's the noun "effect."

drills.title: Who or Whom?
drills.blurb: Subject or object? Try the m-test.

items.prompt: ___ wants the last slice of pizza?
items.explain: You'd answer "HE wants it," so use "who" — he/who, him/whom.

items.prompt: To ___ should I address this letter?
items.explain: After a preposition like "to," use "whom" — you'd say "to him," and him = whom (both end in m).

items.prompt: He is the coach ___ trains our team.
items.explain: "Who" is the subject doing the training — HE trains, so who.

items.prompt: ___ left these muddy boots by the door?
items.explain: Test it: "HE left them" — he means who, him means whom.

items.prompt: With ___ did you travel to Rome?
items.explain: Prepositions like "with" take "whom" — you traveled with HIM, and him = whom.

items.prompt: The author ___ wrote this novel lives nearby.
items.explain: The author is the subject of "wrote" — HE wrote it, so use "who."

items.prompt: The student ___ the teacher praised smiled proudly.
items.explain: The teacher praised HIM, so the object form "whom" is correct (m matches m).

items.prompt: For ___ are these flowers?
items.explain: After the preposition "for," choose "whom" — the flowers are for HIM.

items.prompt: I wonder ___ will win the spelling bee.
items.explain: It's the subject of "will win" — HE will win, so "who."

items.prompt: ___ did the committee choose?
items.explain: The committee chose HIM, so the object form "whom" wins — him/whom both end in m.

items.prompt: He's a mentor ___ many students admire.
items.explain: Students admire HIM, so use the object form "whom."

items.prompt: ___ do you believe deserves the award?
items.explain: Skip "do you believe": HE deserves the award — subject, so "who."

items.prompt: The neighbor ___ we invited brought dessert.
items.explain: We invited HIM, so it's the object "whom" — the him/whom m-match.

items.prompt: ___ scored the winning goal last night?
items.explain: You'd answer "HE scored it" — he means who, him means whom.

items.prompt: From ___ did you borrow this ladder?
items.explain: After the preposition "from," use "whom" — you borrowed it from HIM, and him = whom.

items.prompt: The astronaut ___ commands the mission grew up nearby.
items.explain: The astronaut is the subject of "commands" — HE commands, so "who."

items.prompt: About ___ was this biography written?
items.explain: After the preposition "about," choose "whom" — it was written about HIM.

items.prompt: ___ knows the combination to the safe?
items.explain: Test it: "HE knows it" — the subject form he matches "who."

items.prompt: The candidate ___ the voters trusted won by a landslide.
items.explain: The voters trusted HIM, so the object form "whom" is right — the him/whom m-match.

items.prompt: It was Grandpa ___ taught me to fish.
items.explain: Grandpa is the one doing the teaching — HE taught me, so "who."

items.prompt: ___ did the reporter interview for the story?
items.explain: Flip it: the reporter interviewed HIM — the object form "whom" ends in m, just like him.

items.prompt: I can't remember ___ borrowed my calculator.
items.explain: It's the subject of "borrowed" — HE borrowed it, so "who," even inside a longer sentence.

items.prompt: Beside ___ were you seated at the banquet?
items.explain: "Beside" is a preposition, and prepositions take "whom" — you sat beside HIM.

items.prompt: The jury will decide ___ is telling the truth.
items.explain: The blank is the subject of "is telling" — HE is telling the truth, so "who."

items.prompt: The witness, ___ the lawyers questioned for hours, never wavered.
items.explain: The lawyers questioned HIM — the object of "questioned" takes "whom."

items.prompt: ___ shall I say is calling?
items.explain: Skip "shall I say": HE is calling — the blank is the subject of "is calling," so "who," not the fancy-sounding "whom."

items.prompt: He mentored dozens of pilots, several of ___ now fly for airlines.
items.explain: After "of" — a preposition — it must be "whom": several of THEM, several of whom.

items.prompt: The award goes to the engineer ___, everyone agrees, saved the project.
items.explain: Skip the aside "everyone agrees": HE saved the project — a subject, so "who."

items.prompt: This line is for shoppers with ___ than ten items.
items.explain: Items are countable, so use "fewer"; "less" is for uncountable amounts (less water).

items.prompt: Please add ___ sugar to my tea.
items.explain: Sugar is an uncountable mass, so use "less" — you can't count sugars in your tea.

items.prompt: We saw ___ birds at the feeder today.
items.explain: You can count birds one by one, so countable things take "fewer."

items.prompt: How ___ water should I drink each day?
items.explain: Water is uncountable, so ask "how much"; "how many" is for countable things.

items.prompt: There were ___ cars on the road this morning.
items.explain: Cars can be counted, and countable nouns pair with "fewer."

items.prompt: A large ___ of students joined the club.
items.explain: Students are countable, so it's a "number" of them; "amount" is for uncountable stuff.

items.prompt: I have ___ patience before my morning coffee.
items.explain: Patience is an uncountable quality, so use "less" — you can't count patiences.

items.prompt: How ___ chairs do we need for the party?
items.explain: Chairs are countable, so ask "how many"; save "much" for uncountables.

items.prompt: He saved a surprising ___ money this year.
items.explain: Money is treated as an uncountable mass, so it's an "amount of" money.

items.prompt: The new recipe uses ___ butter.
items.explain: Butter is an uncountable mass, and uncountables always take "less."

items.prompt: ___ than twenty tickets remain for the show.
items.explain: Tickets are countable, so use "fewer" — if you can count them, go fewer.

items.prompt: The ___ volunteers doubled after the news story.
items.explain: Volunteers are countable people, so it's the "number of" volunteers.

items.prompt: Streaming means ___ trips to the video store.
items.explain: Trips are countable events, so countable = "fewer" trips.

items.prompt: ___ mistakes slipped into the second draft.
items.explain: Mistakes can be counted one by one, and countables take "fewer."

items.prompt: How ___ flour do we need for the dough?
items.explain: Flour is an uncountable mass, so ask "how much" — you can't count flours.

items.prompt: The orchard produced ___ apples after the late frost.
items.explain: Apples are countable, and anything you can count takes "fewer."

items.prompt: How ___ stamps are left on the roll?
items.explain: Stamps are countable, so ask "how many" — the plural "are" is your clue.

items.prompt: The trailhead is ___ than ten miles from town.
items.explain: Distance acts as one single stretch, not ten separate miles, so units of measure take "less."

items.prompt: The bike repairs cost ___ than fifty dollars.
items.explain: Money is treated as one lump sum, not fifty separate dollars, so use "less."

items.prompt: A surprising ___ of dust had settled on the bookshelf.
items.explain: Dust is an uncountable mass, so it comes in an "amount" — "number" is for things you can count.

items.prompt: The bakery sold ___ loaves this week but earned more.
items.explain: Loaves are countable items, so it's "fewer" — don't let the money talk pull you toward "less."

items.prompt: There is ___ traffic downtown on Sunday mornings.
items.explain: Traffic is an uncountable mass — you can count cars, but traffic itself takes "less."

items.prompt: He carries ___ tools than his grandfather did.
items.explain: Tools can be counted one by one, so the comparison takes "fewer."

items.prompt: The whole ferry crossing takes ___ than twenty minutes.
items.explain: A span of time is one block, not twenty separate minutes — time, money, and distance take "less."

items.prompt: He finished a huge ___ homework before dinner.
items.explain: Homework is an uncountable mass (you can't say "three homeworks"), so it comes in an "amount of."

items.prompt: Pack ___ luggage if you want room for souvenirs.
items.explain: You can count bags, but "luggage" itself is an uncountable mass — so it takes "less."

items.prompt: How ___ progress has the crew made on the tunnel?
items.explain: Progress is an uncountable quality — no one makes "three progresses" — so ask "how much."

items.prompt: A record ___ entries arrived before the contest deadline.
items.explain: Entries are countable items, so it's a "number of" them — save "amount of" for uncountable stuff.

drills.title: A or An?
drills.blurb: It's about the sound, not the letter.

items.prompt: He carried ___ umbrella in his backpack.
items.explain: "Umbrella" starts with a vowel SOUND (uh), so use "an."

items.prompt: We adopted ___ playful kitten last week.
items.explain: "Playful" starts with a consonant SOUND (p), so "a" is correct.

items.prompt: He ate ___ apple before soccer practice.
items.explain: "Apple" opens with the vowel SOUND "a," so it takes "an."

items.prompt: Dad built ___ treehouse in the backyard.
items.explain: "Treehouse" begins with the consonant SOUND "t," so use "a."

items.prompt: I need ___ eraser for this pencil.
items.explain: "Eraser" starts with the vowel SOUND "ee," so choose "an."

items.prompt: The bread takes ___ hour to bake.
items.explain: The h in "hour" is silent — it SOUNDS like "our," a vowel sound, so "an."

items.prompt: My sister attends ___ university in Ohio.
items.explain: "University" SOUNDS like "yoo," a consonant y-sound, so it takes "a."

items.prompt: He gave ___ honest answer to the judge.
items.explain: The h in "honest" is silent, so it starts with a vowel SOUND — use "an."

items.prompt: The story features ___ unicorn with silver hooves.
items.explain: "Unicorn" begins with the "yoo" SOUND, a consonant sound, so "a" wins.

items.prompt: This coupon is ___ one-time offer.
items.explain: "One" SOUNDS like "won," starting with a w consonant sound, so use "a."

items.prompt: He interviewed ___ FBI agent for his podcast.
items.explain: You say the letter F as "eff" — a vowel SOUND — so it's "an FBI agent."

items.prompt: We hosted ___ European exchange student.
items.explain: "European" starts with the "yoo" SOUND, so despite the E, it takes "a."

items.prompt: The doctor ordered ___ MRI of his knee.
items.explain: M is pronounced "em," a vowel SOUND, so say "an MRI" — go by sound, not spelling.

items.prompt: He peeled ___ orange during halftime.
items.explain: "Orange" opens with a vowel SOUND (or-), so it takes "an."

items.prompt: He plays ___ harmonica on the porch every evening.
items.explain: The h in "harmonica" is fully pronounced — a consonant SOUND — so use "a."

items.prompt: Grandpa carved ___ small canoe from pine.
items.explain: The article matches the very next word — "small" starts with the consonant SOUND "s," so "a."

items.prompt: The duke named his nephew ___ heir to the estate.
items.explain: The h in "heir" is silent — it SOUNDS like "air," a vowel sound, so "an."

items.prompt: The vet took ___ X-ray of the parrot's wing.
items.explain: The letter X is pronounced "ex" — a vowel SOUND — so it's "an X-ray."

items.prompt: The pilot reported ___ UFO over the desert.
items.explain: You say U as "yoo" — a consonant y-SOUND — so despite the vowel letter, it's "a UFO."

items.prompt: Carrying the flag at graduation is ___ honor.
items.explain: The h in "honor" is silent, so the word begins with a vowel SOUND — use "an."

items.prompt: They turned Maple Avenue into ___ one-way street.
items.explain: "One" SOUNDS like "won," beginning with a w consonant sound, so it takes "a."

items.prompt: The stranded sailors sent ___ SOS at midnight.
items.explain: The letter S is pronounced "ess" — a vowel SOUND — so say "an SOS."

items.prompt: He bought ___ used telescope at the flea market.
items.explain: "Used" SOUNDS like "yoozd," starting with a consonant y-sound, so "a" wins.

items.prompt: He scored courtside seats at ___ NBA game.
items.explain: The letter N is pronounced "en" — a vowel SOUND — so it's "an NBA game," by sound, not spelling.

items.prompt: The gelato stand charges ___ euro per scoop.
items.explain: "Euro" begins with the "yoo" SOUND — a consonant y-sound — so it takes "a" despite the E.

items.prompt: The tour visits ___ historic lighthouse on the cape.
items.explain: The h in "historic" is pronounced — a consonant SOUND — so modern usage says "a historic," not "an."

items.prompt: The shelter matched him with ___ 11-year-old beagle.
items.explain: Read the numeral aloud: "eleven" starts with a vowel SOUND, so it's "an 11-year-old."

items.prompt: We booked ___ hotel near the train station.
items.explain: The h in "hotel" is pronounced — a consonant SOUND — so "a hotel"; "an hotel" is an old-fashioned trap.

drills.title: Me or I?
drills.blurb: Pronoun case — cover the other name.

items.prompt: Grandma sent a card to my sister and ___.
items.explain: Drop "my sister": "sent a card to me." Objects take "me," not "I."

items.prompt: My brother and ___ built a sandcastle.
items.explain: Drop "my brother": "I built a sandcastle." Subjects take "I."

items.prompt: The coach picked Sam and ___ for the relay.
items.explain: Remove Sam: "picked me" — you're the object, so use "me."

items.prompt: Mom drove Jess and ___ to school.
items.explain: Drop Jess: "Mom drove me" — objects of a verb take "me."

items.prompt: My friend and ___ love hiking on Saturdays.
items.explain: Drop "my friend": "I love hiking" — the subject needs "I."

items.prompt: ___ washed the dishes together.
items.explain: They're the subject: "He washed" and "I washed," so "He and I."

items.prompt: The teacher thanked ___ for helping.
items.explain: Test each alone: "thanked her," "thanked me" — objects take her/me.

items.prompt: Between you and ___, the test was easy.
items.explain: "Between" is a preposition, and prepositions always take "me" — never "between you and I."

items.prompt: ___ started a book club last spring.
items.explain: It's the subject: drop the friends and "I started" sounds right.

items.prompt: This gift is from Leo and ___.
items.explain: Drop Leo: "from me" — after a preposition like "from," use "me."

items.prompt: ___ are entering the science fair.
items.explain: Subjects use she/I: test each alone — "She is entering," "I am entering."

items.prompt: The photo shows my cousins and ___ at the lake.
items.explain: Drop the cousins: "the photo shows me" — the object takes "me."

items.prompt: The neighbors invited ___ to dinner.
items.explain: Test each: "invited him," "invited me" — objects of the verb take him/me.

items.prompt: Uncle Ray taught my cousin and ___ to whittle.
items.explain: Drop the cousin: "taught me" — objects of the verb take "me."

items.prompt: Nadia and ___ painted the fence bright green.
items.explain: Drop Nadia: "I painted the fence" — subjects take "I."

items.prompt: The bus driver waved at Milo and ___.
items.explain: Remove Milo: "waved at me" — after a preposition like "at," use "me."

items.prompt: ___ waited in line all night for concert tickets.
items.explain: Test each alone: "He waited" and "I waited" — subjects take he/I.

items.prompt: The judges awarded ___ first prize in the bake-off.
items.explain: Test each alone: "awarded her," "awarded me" — objects of the verb take her/me.

items.prompt: ___ kids always get the back seats on field trips.
items.explain: Cover the noun: "We get the back seats" — the subject stays "we" even with "kids" attached.

items.prompt: The coach let ___ seniors lead the warm-up.
items.explain: Cover the noun: "let us lead" — the object stays "us" even with "seniors" attached.

items.prompt: ___, this chili could use more salt.
items.explain: "Between" is a preposition, and prepositions demand object pronouns — "between you and I" is always wrong.

items.prompt: Aunt Rosa mailed postcards to Felix and ___.
items.explain: Drop Felix: "mailed postcards to me" — the preposition "to" takes "me."

items.prompt: The twins and ___ rebuilt the go-kart engine.
items.explain: Drop the twins: "I rebuilt the engine" — the subject needs "I."

items.prompt: ___ volunteer at the animal shelter on Fridays.
items.explain: Test each alone: "She volunteers" and "I volunteer" — subjects take she/I.

items.prompt: The reporter interviewed ___ right after the match.
items.explain: Test each alone: "interviewed him," "interviewed me" — objects take him/me, no matter how formal "he and I" sounds.

items.prompt: ___ neighbors organized the whole block party.
items.explain: Cover the noun: "We organized" — never "Us organized" — so the subject is "We neighbors."

items.prompt: The scoutmaster trusted Wei and ___ with the map.
items.explain: Drop Wei: "trusted me with the map" — the verb's object takes "me."

items.prompt: My lab partner and ___ retested every sample.
items.explain: Drop the partner: "I retested every sample" — subjects always take "I."

items.prompt: Everyone came ___ the twins, who were sick.
items.explain: "Except" means "excluding"; "accept" means "to receive." Except = exit/leave out.

items.prompt: Don't ___ your keys again!
items.explain: "Lose" means to misplace; "loose" means not tight. Lose lost an o!

items.prompt: I wonder ___ it will rain today.
items.explain: "Whether" introduces a choice or doubt; "weather" is rain, sun, and snow.

items.prompt: He gave me a kind ___ on my haircut.
items.explain: A compliment is praise (I like it); a complement completes something.

items.prompt: ___ jacket is this on the chair?
items.explain: "Whose" shows ownership; "who's" is short for "who is."

items.prompt: The school ___ greeted students at the door.
items.explain: The princiPAL is your pal; a principle is a rule or belief.

items.prompt: He wrote thank-you notes on fancy ___.
items.explain: StationEry is for Envelopes; stationAry means stAying still.

items.prompt: The parade ___ our house at noon.
items.explain: "Passed" is the verb (it moved by); "past" is a noun, adjective, or preposition.

items.prompt: The guide ___ us through the museum yesterday.
items.explain: The past tense of "lead" is "led"; "lead" (rhyming with led) is the metal.

items.prompt: Let's discuss the budget ___ at tomorrow's meeting.
items.explain: "Further" is for degree or extent (discussing something more); "farther" is only for physical distance (a mile farther down the road).

items.prompt: The new rule had a big ___ on traffic.
items.explain: "Effect" is usually the noun (the result); "affect" is usually the verb (to influence).

items.prompt: Double-check to ___ the door is locked.
items.explain: "Ensure" means to make certain; "insure" is what insurance companies do.

items.prompt: The teacher's question failed to ___ any answers.
items.explain: "Elicit" (verb) means to draw out; "illicit" (adjective) means illegal — ill = bad.

items.prompt: Please be ___ about the surprise party.
items.explain: "Discreet" means tactfully quiet; "discrete" means separate — its two e's stay apart.

items.prompt: Remember to ___ your sources in the essay.
items.explain: "Cite" means to quote a source; a "site" is a place, and "sight" is vision.

items.prompt: The poem makes an ___ to Greek myth.
items.explain: An allusion is an indirect reference; an illusion is a false impression or trick.

items.prompt: We had chocolate cake for ___ after dinner.
items.explain: Dessert has two s's because you always want seconds; a desert is dry, sandy land.

items.prompt: Press the ___ pedal gently to slow the car.
items.explain: A brake stops a car; to break is to smash or snap something.

items.prompt: I can't ___ to watch scary movies alone.
items.explain: "Bear" means to endure or carry; "bare" means uncovered or naked.

items.prompt: We boarded the ___ an hour before takeoff.
items.explain: A plane flies; "plain" means simple or a flat stretch of land.

items.prompt: He won the lead ___ in the school play.
items.explain: A role is a part you play; a roll is bread, a list, or a tumble.

items.prompt: ___ did you park the car this morning?
items.explain: "Where" asks about a place — it has "here" inside it; "wear" is what you do with clothes.

items.prompt: The ___ of the farm egg was bright orange.
items.explain: The yolk is the yellow of an egg; a yoke is the wooden bar that harnesses oxen.

items.prompt: The coach gave him solid ___ before the tryout.
items.explain: Advice with a c is the noun (the thing you give); advise with an s is the verb (the act of giving it).

items.prompt: Lawmakers gathered inside the ___ building to vote.
items.explain: Capitol with an o is only the building — picture its round dome; capital covers everything else (city, money, letters).

items.prompt: The city ___ voted to build a new skate park.
items.explain: A council is a group that meets and votes; counsel means advice or the lawyer who gives it.

items.prompt: The sandpaper felt rough and ___ under my fingers.
items.explain: Coarse means rough in texture; a course is a class, a path, or part of a meal.

items.prompt: Charge your ___ before the long flight.
items.explain: Device with a c is the noun (the gadget); devise with an s is the verb meaning to invent a plan.

items.prompt: The bride walked slowly down the ___.
items.explain: An aisle is a walkway between seats; an isle is a small island.

items.prompt: Candles flickered on the ___ at the front of the church.
items.explain: An altar (noun) is the table in a church; to alter (verb) is to change something.

items.prompt: He has a real ___ for telling stories.
items.explain: Flair is natural talent or style; a flare is a burst of light or a widening shape.

items.prompt: He tied the apron snugly around his ___.
items.explain: Your waist is the middle of your body; waste is garbage or careless loss.

items.prompt: Carefully ___ the batter into the pan.
items.explain: You pour a liquid; you pore over a book (study it closely), and pores are tiny openings in skin.

items.prompt: The strange headline managed to ___ my curiosity.
items.explain: "Pique" means to stir up interest; a peak is a mountaintop, and a peek is a quick look.

items.prompt: His grandparents decided to ___ from Italy in 1920.
items.explain: Emigrate = Exit your country; immigrate = come In to a new one — "from Italy" signals the exit.

items.prompt: The repair costs were ___ entirely by the taxpayers.
items.explain: "Borne" is the past participle of bear (carried, endured); "born" is only for birth.

items.prompt: Volunteers will ___ the neighborhood asking for votes.
items.explain: To canvass (double s) is to go door to door seeking support; canvas is the sturdy cloth.

items.prompt: A ___ of tourists poured into the tiny plaza.
items.explain: A horde is a large crowd; a hoard is a hidden stash — a dragon hoards gold.

items.prompt: The spicy curry delighted his ___.
items.explain: Your palate is your sense of taste, a palette holds a painter's colors, and a pallet is a shipping platform.

items.prompt: The trailer is designed to ___ your appetite for the movie.
items.explain: To whet is to sharpen — you whet an appetite like a blade; "wet" just means soaked.

drills.title: One Word or Two?
drills.blurb: everyday vs. every day, and friends.

items.prompt: I wear these shoes ___ to work.
items.explain: "Every day" (two words) = each day; "everyday" (one word) is an adjective meaning ordinary.

items.prompt: The cat jumped ___ the box.
items.explain: "Into" (one word) shows movement from outside to inside.

items.prompt: ___ we should leave a bit earlier.
items.explain: "Maybe" (one word) means "perhaps"; "may be" is a verb phrase, as in "it may be true."

items.prompt: The movie had ___ started when we arrived.
items.explain: "Already" means "before now"; "all ready" means everyone is prepared.

items.prompt: I'm proud to be ___ of this team.
items.explain: "A part" (two words) means a piece of; "apart" (one word) means separated.

items.prompt: These are just my ___ sneakers.
items.explain: Before a noun, use the adjective "everyday" (ordinary); "every day" answers "when?"

items.prompt: The cat leaped ___ the kitchen counter.
items.explain: "Onto" (one word) shows movement to a surface.

items.prompt: Let's rest for ___ before hiking on.
items.explain: After a preposition like "for," use the noun "a while"; "awhile" is an adverb.

items.prompt: Would you like ___ soup?
items.explain: "Any more" (two words) means an additional amount; "anymore" means "nowadays."

items.prompt: Sing the chorus ___, everyone!
items.explain: "All together" means as a group; "altogether" means entirely.

items.prompt: He came ___ say hello.
items.explain: Here "in" goes with "came" and "to" starts "to say" — keep them apart.

items.prompt: This ___ our best chance to win.
items.explain: The sentence needs a verb: "may be" (might be); "maybe" only means "perhaps."

items.prompt: Let's grab lunch ___ next week.
items.explain: "Sometime" means at an unspecified point; "some time" means a stretch of time.

items.prompt: After the quiz, we moved ___ chapter five.
items.explain: "Move on" is the phrasal verb, so "on" stays separate from "to."

items.prompt: ___ in the office got a bonus this year.
items.explain: "Everyone" (one word) means all the people; "every one" points to each separate item.

items.prompt: Has ___ seen my umbrella?
items.explain: "Anyone" (one word) means any person; "any one" means any single item from a set.

items.prompt: I ___ find my glasses anywhere.
items.explain: "Cannot" is the standard one-word form; "can not" appears only in rare emphatic phrasing.

items.prompt: He keeps a ___ of his photos on an external drive.
items.explain: As a noun, it's one word: a "backup"; "back up" (two words) is the verb.

items.prompt: Remember to ___ your laptop before the update.
items.explain: As a verb, use two words: you "back up" files; "backup" is the noun or adjective.

items.prompt: He typed his username on the ___ page.
items.explain: Before a noun like "page," use the one-word adjective "login"; "log in" is the verb.

items.prompt: You need to ___ before you can post a comment.
items.explain: As a verb, it's two words: you "log in"; "login" is the noun or adjective.

items.prompt: ___ of the twelve cupcakes was gone by noon.
items.explain: "Every one" (two words) means each individual item — cupcakes, not people.

items.prompt: You may borrow ___ of these three books.
items.explain: "Any one" (two words) means any single item from a set; "anyone" refers to a person.

items.prompt: The repair costs were ___ too high.
items.explain: "Altogether" (one word) means entirely; "all together" means as a group.

items.prompt: The ___ tail wagged happily when we got home.
items.explain: One dog owns the tail, so the apostrophe goes before the s — dog's.

items.prompt: We ___ have class on Friday afternoons.
items.explain: The apostrophe replaces the missing o in 'do not,' so it sits exactly where the letter dropped out: don't.

items.prompt: ___ starting to rain, so grab an umbrella.
items.explain: You can swap in 'it is,' so you need the contraction it's — and its' is never a word.

items.prompt: Three ___ sat on the fence at sunset.
items.explain: Nothing is owned here — it's just a plain plural, and plurals never take an apostrophe.

items.prompt: I ___ wait for the science fair next week.
items.explain: The apostrophe marks the letters dropped from 'cannot,' landing between n and t: can't.

items.prompt: The robot slowly lowered ___ mechanical arm.
items.explain: Possessive its has no apostrophe — if 'it is' doesn't fit the sentence, skip the apostrophe.

items.prompt: The ___ locker room is down the hall on the left.
items.explain: The room belongs to many girls, so the apostrophe follows the plural s: girls'.

items.prompt: ___ bringing the snacks to practice tomorrow?
items.explain: You can swap in 'who is,' so the contraction who's is correct.

items.prompt: ___ backpack is this sitting by the door?
items.explain: 'Who is backpack' makes no sense, so you need the possessive whose — no apostrophe.

items.prompt: Our two ___ names are Ms. Lee and Mr. Cruz.
items.explain: Two teachers share the names, so make the word plural first, then add the apostrophe after the s: teachers'.

items.prompt: The ___ museum opens at nine on Saturdays.
items.explain: 'Children' is already plural with no s, so it takes a regular 's — the apostrophe never follows a letter that isn't there.

items.prompt: We watered the ___ garden while they were traveling.
items.explain: The whole family ('they') owns the garden, so pluralize Jones to Joneses, then add the apostrophe after: the Joneses'.

items.prompt: ___ bicycle has a flat tire again.
items.explain: For a singular name ending in s, add 's after the whole name (James's) — never move the apostrophe inside the name itself.

items.prompt: ___ going to the library right after school.
items.explain: You can swap in "we are," so the apostrophe replaces the missing a: we're.

items.prompt: The ___ mane was tangled with burrs.
items.explain: One horse owns the mane, so the apostrophe goes before the s: horse's.

items.prompt: ___ not fair that he always goes first.
items.explain: "That is" fits the sentence, so you need the contraction that's.

items.prompt: Two ___ flew past the kitchen window.
items.explain: Nothing is owned — it's a plain plural, and plurals never take an apostrophe.

items.prompt: My ___ car is parked in the driveway.
items.explain: One brother owns the car, so it's apostrophe-then-s: brother's.

items.prompt: Both ___ bikes were left out in the rain.
items.explain: "Both" tells you there are two boys, so make the plural first, then hang the apostrophe after the s: boys'.

items.prompt: You ___ forget your lines on opening night.
items.explain: The apostrophe sits exactly where the o of "not" dropped out — between n and t: shouldn't.

items.prompt: The ___ engine roared as it left the station.
items.explain: One train owns the engine, so the apostrophe comes before the s: train's.

items.prompt: All three ___ lockers were decorated before the game.
items.explain: Three players own the lockers, so the apostrophe follows the plural s: players'.

items.prompt: ___ already seen that movie twice this month.
items.explain: Here he's is short for "he has" — contractions can hide has as well as is.

items.prompt: The ___ department is on the second floor of the store.
items.explain: "Men" is already plural without an s, so it takes a regular 's — mens' puts the apostrophe after a letter that was never there.

items.prompt: The ___ choice award went to a local bakery.
items.explain: "People" is an irregular plural with no s, so the possessive is simply people's.

items.prompt: We're invited to the ___ barbecue on Saturday.
items.explain: The whole family hosts it, so pluralize the name first (the Smiths), then add the apostrophe after: the Smiths'.

items.prompt: We leave for camp in two ___ time.
items.explain: Time expressions take a possessive — two weeks own the time — so plural weeks gets its apostrophe after the s.

items.prompt: Both ___ offices overlook the park.
items.explain: Two bosses share the offices: pluralize boss to bosses, then add the apostrophe after the s — bosses'.

items.prompt: The plural of "mouse" (the animal) is ___.
items.explain: "Mouse" → "mice." (The computer gadget is often "mouses," but the animal is always "mice.")

items.prompt: The plural of "goose" is ___.
items.explain: "Goose" → "geese" — the oo flips to ee, just like tooth → teeth.

items.prompt: The plural of "child" is ___.
items.explain: "Child" → "children" — an old English -en plural, like oxen.

items.prompt: The plural of "foot" is ___.
items.explain: "Foot" → "feet" — the vowel changes; never add -s on top.

items.prompt: The plural of "tooth" is ___.
items.explain: "Tooth" → "teeth" — oo becomes ee, same pattern as goose → geese.

items.prompt: The everyday plural of "person" is ___.
items.explain: "Person" → "people" in everyday use; "peoples" means multiple ethnic groups.

items.prompt: The plural of "leaf" is ___.
items.explain: "Leaf" → "leaves" — the f softens to v, like knife → knives.

items.prompt: The plural of "deer" is ___.
items.explain: "Deer" doesn't change — like sheep, one deer or ten deer.

items.prompt: The classic Latin plural of "cactus" is ___.
items.explain: Latin -us often becomes -i: cactus → cacti, fungus → fungi.

items.prompt: The plural of "ox" is ___.
items.explain: "Ox" → "oxen" — one of the last surviving -en plurals, like children.

items.prompt: The plural of "phenomenon" is ___.
items.explain: Greek -on becomes -a: one phenomenon, two phenomena.

items.prompt: The plural of "criterion" is ___.
items.explain: One criterion, many criteria — same Greek -on → -a shift as phenomenon.

items.prompt: The plural of "analysis" is ___.
items.explain: Greek -is becomes -es: analysis → analyses, crisis → crises.

items.prompt: The plural of "knife" is ___.
items.explain: "Knife" → "knives" — the f softens to v, just like leaf → leaves.

items.prompt: The plural of "wife" is ___.
items.explain: "Wife" → "wives" — the f-to-v switch, same family as knife → knives.

items.prompt: The plural of "life" is ___.
items.explain: "Life" → "lives" — a cat has nine lives, never nine lifes.

items.prompt: The plural of "wolf" is ___.
items.explain: "Wolf" → "wolves" — f becomes v before -es, like shelf → shelves.

items.prompt: The plural of "shelf" is ___.
items.explain: "Shelf" → "shelves" — the f flips to v, same pattern as wolf → wolves.

items.prompt: The plural of "half" is ___.
items.explain: "Half" → "halves" — cut two apples into four halves, never halfs.

items.prompt: The plural of "loaf" is ___.
items.explain: "Loaf" → "loaves" — the baker sells loaves, with f turning to v.

items.prompt: The plural of "thief" is ___.
items.explain: "Thief" → "thieves" — f becomes v, and keep the i-before-e spelling.

items.prompt: The plural of "potato" is ___.
items.explain: Consonant + o usually takes -es: potato → potatoes (an apostrophe never makes a plural).

items.prompt: The plural of "tomato" is ___.
items.explain: "Tomato" → "tomatoes" — like potato, it needs -es, not just -s.

items.prompt: The plural of "hero" is ___.
items.explain: "Hero" → "heroes" — consonant + o adds -es, same as potato → potatoes.

items.prompt: The plural of "echo" is ___.
items.explain: "Echo" → "echoes" — another consonant + o word that takes -es.

items.prompt: The plural of "aircraft" is ___.
items.explain: "Aircraft" doesn't change — one aircraft or a fleet of aircraft, like deer.

items.prompt: The plural of "series" is ___.
items.explain: "Series" stays the same — one TV series or five series, no change.

items.prompt: The plural of "crisis" is ___.
items.explain: Greek -is becomes -es: crisis → crises, same as analysis → analyses.

items.prompt: The plural of "thesis" is ___.
items.explain: "Thesis" → "theses" — the Greek -is → -es shift, like crisis → crises.

items.prompt: The plural of "bacterium" is ___.
items.explain: Latin -um becomes -a: one bacterium, millions of bacteria.

items.prompt: In mass communication, the plural of "medium" is ___.
items.explain: Medium → media for channels of communication; "mediums" is reserved for fortune-tellers.

items.prompt: The classic Latin plural of "radius" is ___.
items.explain: Latin -us becomes -i: radius → radii, the standard form in geometry.

items.prompt: The plural of "alumnus" (a male graduate) is ___.
items.explain: Alumnus → alumni (Latin -us → -i); "alumnae" is the plural of the feminine "alumna."

items.prompt: The classic Latin plural of "appendix" is ___.
items.explain: Latin -ix becomes -ices: appendix → appendices, the usual form for book sections.

items.prompt: In mathematics, the plural of "matrix" is ___.
items.explain: Matrix → matrices — the same -ix → -ices shift as appendix → appendices.

items.prompt: Yesterday we ___ (to swim) across the lake.
items.explain: Simple past of "swim" is "swam"; "swum" needs a helper ("have swum").

items.prompt: Yesterday he ___ (to go) home early.
items.explain: Simple past of "go" is "went"; "gone" needs a helper ("has gone").

items.prompt: We ___ (to eat) pancakes this morning.
items.explain: Simple past of "eat" is "ate"; "eaten" needs a helper ("have eaten").

items.prompt: I ___ (to see) a shooting star last night.
items.explain: Simple past of "see" is "saw"; "seen" needs a helper ("have seen").

items.prompt: He ___ (to bring) snacks to the picnic yesterday.
items.explain: "Bring" → "brought" — think of its rhyme buddy: buy → bought.

items.prompt: Last year he ___ (to teach) third grade.
items.explain: "Teach" → "taught" — same pattern as catch → caught.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to drink) all the lemonade.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "drunk"; "drank" is the simple past.

items.prompt: The show has already ___ (to begin).
items.explain: After "has," use "begun"; "began" stands alone ("it began at noon").

items.prompt: Someone has ___ (to break) the vase.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "broken"; "broke" is the simple past.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to write) three novels.
items.explain: After "has," use "written"; "wrote" stands alone ("he wrote it last year").

items.prompt: The phone ___ (to ring) twice during dinner.
items.explain: Simple past of "ring" is "rang"; "rung" needs a helper ("had rung").

items.prompt: Yesterday he ___ (to catch) the last bus.
items.explain: "Catch" → "caught" — same pattern as teach → taught.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to lie) on the couch all day.
items.explain: To lie (recline) goes lie/lay/lain; "laid" belongs to "lay" (to place something).

items.prompt: He ___ (to lay) the book on the table.
items.explain: To lay (place something) goes lay/laid/laid — it always takes an object.

items.prompt: By noon, they had ___ (to swim) two miles.
items.explain: After "had," use the participle "swum"; "swam" is the simple past.

items.prompt: Yesterday he ___ (to come) home late.
items.explain: Simple past of "come" is "came"; "come" is the participle ("has come").

items.prompt: He ___ (to find) his keys under the sofa last night.
items.explain: Simple past of "find" is "found" — never "finded".

items.prompt: He ___ (to give) me his old bike last week.
items.explain: Simple past of "give" is "gave"; "given" needs a helper ("has given").

items.prompt: The tomatoes ___ (to grow) fast last summer.
items.explain: Simple past of "grow" is "grew"; "grown" needs a helper ("have grown").

items.prompt: He ___ (to know) all the answers on last week's test.
items.explain: Simple past of "know" is "knew"; "known" needs a helper ("has known").

items.prompt: He ___ (to make) dinner for us last night.
items.explain: Simple past of "make" is "made" — never "maked".

items.prompt: He ___ (to sell) his car last month.
items.explain: "Sell" → "sold" — same pattern as tell → told.

items.prompt: Yesterday we ___ (to sit) in the front row.
items.explain: Simple past of "sit" is "sat" — never "sitted".

items.prompt: Our team ___ (to win) the game on Saturday.
items.explain: Simple past of "win" is "won" — never "winned".

items.prompt: He ___ (to sleep) ten hours last night.
items.explain: "Sleep" → "slept" — same pattern as keep → kept.

items.prompt: He ___ (to send) the letter yesterday.
items.explain: "Send" → "sent" — same pattern as spend → spent.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to choose) a topic for his essay.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "chosen"; "chose" is the simple past.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to drive) that truck for years.
items.explain: After "has," use "driven"; "drove" stands alone ("he drove home").

items.prompt: The birds ___ (to fly) south last October.
items.explain: Simple past of "fly" is "flew"; "flown" needs a helper ("have flown").

items.prompt: He ___ (to fall) off his bike yesterday.
items.explain: Simple past of "fall" is "fell"; "fallen" needs a helper ("has fallen").

items.prompt: He has ___ (to forget) his password again.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "forgotten"; "forgot" is the simple past.

items.prompt: The pond has ___ (to freeze) solid.
items.explain: After "has," use "frozen"; "froze" stands alone ("it froze overnight").

items.prompt: He has ___ (to hide) the presents in the closet.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "hidden"; "hid" is the simple past.

items.prompt: He ___ (to keep) every ticket stub from last season's games.
items.explain: "Keep" → "kept" — same pattern as sleep → slept.

items.prompt: He ___ (to leave) his umbrella on the train yesterday.
items.explain: Simple past of "leave" is "left" — never "leaved".

items.prompt: He ___ (to lose) his wallet last weekend.
items.explain: Simple past of "lose" is "lost" — never "losed".

items.prompt: We ___ (to meet) at summer camp years ago.
items.explain: Simple past of "meet" is "met" — never "meeted".

items.prompt: He has ___ (to speak) with the principal already.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "spoken"; "spoke" is the simple past.

items.prompt: He ___ (to spend) all his allowance yesterday.
items.explain: "Spend" → "spent" — same pattern as send → sent.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to throw) the ball over the fence.
items.explain: After "has," use "thrown"; "threw" stands alone ("he threw it far").

items.prompt: The sun ___ (to rise) at six this morning.
items.explain: To rise (go up on its own) goes rise/rose/risen; "raised" belongs to "raise" (to lift something).

items.prompt: He ___ (to raise) his hand to ask a question.
items.explain: To raise (lift something) is regular — raise/raised/raised — and always takes an object.

items.prompt: He had ___ (to hang) the picture above the fireplace.
items.explain: Objects are "hung"; "hanged" is reserved for executions.

items.prompt: The ship had ___ (to sink) before help arrived.
items.explain: After "had," use the participle "sunk"; "sank" is the simple past.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to sing) that song a hundred times.
items.explain: After "has," use "sung"; "sang" stands alone ("he sang it yesterday").

items.prompt: He has ___ (to shake) hands with the mayor twice.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "shaken"; "shook" is the simple past.

items.prompt: He has ___ (to tear) his jacket on the fence.
items.explain: After "has," use "torn"; "tore" stands alone ("he tore it yesterday").

items.prompt: The witness has ___ (to swear) to tell the truth.
items.explain: After "has," use the participle "sworn"; "swore" is the simple past.

items.prompt: He had ___ (to wake) before dawn every day that week.
items.explain: After "had," use the participle "woken"; "woke" is the simple past.

items.prompt: Last winter the crew ___ (to fell) the dead pines.
items.explain: To fell (cut down) is regular — fell/felled/felled; "fell" is the past of "fall."

drills.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
drills.blurb: Match the verb past the distractions.

items.prompt: The chocolates in that box ___ almost gone.
items.explain: The subject is "chocolates" (plural); ignore the "in that box" phrase, so the verb is "are."

items.prompt: The team ___ practicing every morning this week.
items.explain: A collective noun like "team" acts as one unit, so it takes the singular "is."

items.prompt: The singers in the choir ___ excited about the concert.
items.explain: The subject is "singers" (plural), not the nearby "choir" — so use "are."

items.prompt: Here ___ the keys to the cabin.
items.explain: In "here/there" sentences the real subject comes after the verb — "keys" is plural, so use "are."

items.prompt: The captain and the coach ___ meeting after practice.
items.explain: Two subjects joined by "and" make a plural subject, so the verb is "are."

items.prompt: Each of the puzzles ___ a hidden twist.
items.explain: "Each" is singular no matter what follows it, so the verb is "has."

items.prompt: Neither the twins nor their cousin ___ ever seen snow.
items.explain: With "neither…nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject — "cousin" is singular, so "has."

items.prompt: Either the librarian or the volunteers ___ the shelves each night.
items.explain: With "either…or," match the nearer subject — "volunteers" is plural, so "tidy."

items.prompt: Ten dollars ___ a fair price for that puzzle.
items.explain: An amount of money treated as one sum is singular, so "ten dollars is."

items.prompt: There ___ several letters on the desk.
items.explain: In a "there ___" sentence the verb agrees with what follows; "letters" is plural, so "are."

items.prompt: Neither of the recipes ___ any sugar.
items.explain: "Neither" on its own is singular — the "of the recipes" phrase doesn't change that.

items.prompt: The paintings in the west gallery ___ restored last spring.
items.explain: The subject is the plural "paintings" — "in the west gallery" is just a decoy phrase.

items.prompt: ___ either of these keys open the shed?
items.explain: "Either" is singular, so the question needs "Does," even with two keys in view.

items.prompt: Twenty minutes ___ all the time we need for warm-ups.
items.explain: A span of time treated as a single block takes a singular verb: "twenty minutes is."

items.prompt: The boxes of cereal ___ on sale this week.
items.explain: The subject is the plural "boxes" — "of cereal" is just a distractor — so use "are."

items.prompt: The jury ___ finally reached a verdict.
items.explain: A collective noun like "jury" acts as one body, so it takes the singular "has."

items.prompt: Many of the seats ___ still empty when the curtain rose.
items.explain: "Many" is always plural, so it takes "were."

items.prompt: The hammer and the saw ___ back in the toolbox.
items.explain: Two subjects joined by "and" make a plural subject, so the verb is "are."

items.prompt: Everyone in the parade ___ the full two miles.
items.explain: "Everyone" is singular no matter how big the crowd, so it takes "walks."

items.prompt: The bouquet of roses ___ fresh water.
items.explain: The subject is the singular "bouquet," not the nearby "roses," so use "needs."

items.prompt: The pilot, along with the passengers, ___ ready for takeoff.
items.explain: "Along with" does not make a compound subject — the subject is still just "pilot," so use "was."

items.prompt: Both of the bridges ___ repairs after the flood.
items.explain: "Both" is always plural, so it takes "need."

items.prompt: Few of the students ___ homework on Friday nights.
items.explain: "Few" is always plural, so it takes "do."

items.prompt: ___ there any tickets left for the matinee?
items.explain: In a "there" sentence the verb agrees with what follows — "tickets" is plural, so "Are."

items.prompt: Two-thirds of the pizza ___ already gone.
items.explain: With a fraction, the verb agrees with the noun after "of" — "pizza" is singular, so "is."

items.prompt: Either the director or the actors ___ the final say on costumes.
items.explain: With "either…or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject — "actors" is plural, so "have."

items.prompt: Neither the players nor their coach ___ a copy of the schedule.
items.explain: With "neither…nor," match the nearer subject — "coach" is singular, so "has."

items.prompt: Macaroni and cheese ___ his favorite dinner.
items.explain: "Macaroni and cheese" names one dish, so despite the "and" it takes the singular "is."

items.prompt: Nearly half of the apples ___ bruised in shipping.
items.explain: With a fraction, agree with the noun after "of" — "apples" is plural, so "were."

items.prompt: "Great Expectations" ___ still on the summer reading list.
items.explain: The title of a single work is singular even when it looks plural, so use "is."

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: We came, we saw, we conquered.
We came we saw we conquered.
We came, we saw we, conquered.
items.explain: Three short parallel independent clauses take commas between them (a classic exception to the comma-splice rule).

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: We packed apples, pretzels, and juice.
We packed apples pretzels and juice.
We packed, apples, pretzels and juice.
items.explain: Separate items in a series with commas — but never put a comma between the verb and its first item.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.explain: A comma before a name shows you're speaking TO Grandma, not planning to eat her — the direct-address comma saves lives.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: I studied hard, and I passed the test.
I studied hard and, I passed the test.
I studied hard, and, I passed the test.
items.explain: When 'and' joins two complete sentences, the comma goes BEFORE the conjunction, never after.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: After the movie, we walked home.
After the movie we walked, home.
After, the movie we walked home.
items.explain: An introductory phrase takes a comma right where it ends — where you'd naturally pause before the main clause.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
It was raining, we stayed inside.
It was raining so, we stayed inside.
items.explain: Two complete sentences can't be joined by a comma alone (a comma splice) — you need the conjunction 'so' right after the comma.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: My uncle, who lives in Ohio, visits every summer.
My uncle who lives in Ohio, visits every summer.
My uncle, who lives in Ohio visits every summer.
items.explain: A nonessential clause needs commas on BOTH sides — think of them as handles you could use to lift the clause out.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.explain: Commas go between the items in a list — never between a subject and its first verb, and never right after 'and.'

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: I think, Maria, you dropped this.
I think Maria you dropped this.
I think, Maria you dropped this.
items.explain: A name in direct address gets commas on both sides when it interrupts the sentence.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The bell rang, and everyone hurried out.
The bell rang, everyone hurried out.
The bell rang and everyone, hurried out.
items.explain: A comma alone can't glue two sentences together — pair it with a coordinating conjunction like 'and.'

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Paris, which is in France, has great museums.
Paris which is in France has great museums.
Paris, which is in France has great museums.
items.explain: There's only one Paris, so the clause is extra information and must be fenced off by commas on both sides.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: My friend Lena, a violinist, won first prize.
My friend Lena a violinist, won first prize.
My friend, Lena, a violinist won first prize.
items.explain: The appositive 'a violinist' renames Lena and needs a comma on each side, like parentheses.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: He opened the door and stepped outside.
He opened the door, and stepped outside.
He opened the door and, stepped outside.
items.explain: No comma before 'and' here — 'stepped outside' has no subject of its own, so it's one sentence with two verbs, not two sentences.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: When the bell rings, line up quietly.
When the bell rings line up quietly.
When, the bell rings, line up quietly.
items.explain: A dependent clause that starts the sentence is followed by a comma right where it ends.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.explain: When the dependent clause comes AFTER the main clause, no comma is needed before it.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The game is on Friday, June 5.
The game is on Friday June 5.
The game is on, Friday, June 5.
items.explain: Put a comma between the day of the week and the date, but never after 'on.'

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.explain: A comma separates the quotation from 'he said,' and in American style it goes INSIDE the closing quotation mark.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: It was a cold, windy day.
It was a cold windy day.
It was a cold, windy, day.
items.explain: Coordinate adjectives ('cold AND windy' works) take a comma between them — but never before the noun.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.explain: Cumulative adjectives like 'three small' build on each other ('three AND small' fails the test), so no comma.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: It was late; however, he kept reading.
It was late, however, he kept reading.
It was late however, he kept reading.
items.explain: 'However' between two sentences needs a semicolon before it and a comma after — a comma alone makes a splice.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: He trained daily; therefore, he improved fast.
He trained daily, therefore, he improved fast.
He trained daily therefore he improved fast.
items.explain: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so it needs a semicolon before it, not just a comma.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: They moved to Austin, Texas, last year.
They moved to Austin Texas last year.
They moved to Austin, Texas last year.
items.explain: A state after a city takes commas on BOTH sides — the one after 'Texas' is required, not optional.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: On July 4, 1776, the Declaration was signed.
On July 4 1776, the Declaration was signed.
On July 4, 1776 the Declaration was signed.
items.explain: In a full date, the year gets a comma before AND after it when the sentence continues.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Students who study daily earn better grades.
Students, who study daily, earn better grades.
Students who study daily, earn better grades.
items.explain: This clause is restrictive — it tells WHICH students — so it takes no commas at all.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.explain: You have only one hometown, so the appositive 'Omaha' is extra information and needs a comma before it.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The recipe, of course, calls for sugar.
The recipe of course, calls for sugar.
The recipe, of course calls for sugar.
items.explain: An interrupter like 'of course' gets commas on BOTH sides, never just one.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: He bought an old silver coin.
He bought an old, silver coin.
He bought an, old silver coin.
items.explain: Age and material adjectives stack cumulatively ('old AND silver coin' sounds wrong), so no comma between them.

items.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Send it to 42 Elm Street, Dayton, Ohio.
Send it to 42 Elm Street Dayton, Ohio.
Send it to 42 Elm, Street, Dayton, Ohio.
items.explain: In an address, commas separate street from city and city from state — but never split the street name itself.

drills.title: Capitalization
drills.blurb: Proper nouns, titles, and sentence starts.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: We visited Aunt Mary in the spring.
We visited aunt Mary in the Spring.
We visited Aunt mary in the spring.
items.explain: "Aunt Mary" is a proper name (capitalized); seasons like "spring" stay lowercase.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
items.explain: Days of the week AND months are always capitalized — both are proper nouns.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: Yesterday I rode my bike to the park.
yesterday I rode my bike to the park.
Yesterday i rode my bike to the park.
items.explain: Capitalize the first word of every sentence, and the pronoun 'I' is capitalized everywhere, always.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: We crossed the Golden Gate Bridge at sunset.
We crossed the golden gate bridge at sunset.
We crossed the Golden Gate bridge at sunset.
items.explain: Capitalize every word of a specific place's full name — 'Bridge' is part of the name, so it gets a capital too.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: He speaks Spanish and English at home.
He speaks spanish and english at home.
He speaks Spanish and english at home.
items.explain: Languages and nationalities are proper nouns, so both Spanish and English take capitals.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: President Lincoln delivered a short speech.
president Lincoln delivered a short speech.
President lincoln delivered a short speech.
items.explain: A title used right before a name becomes part of the name — capitalize both 'President' and 'Lincoln.'

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: Every club elects a president each fall.
Every club elects a President each fall.
every club elects a president each fall.
items.explain: With no name attached, 'president' is just a job word — lowercase, like 'teacher' or 'coach.'

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: Drive north for two miles, then turn left.
Drive North for two miles, then turn left.
drive north for two miles, then turn left.
items.explain: Compass directions stay lowercase when they just tell you which way to go.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: My cousins live in the South.
My cousins live in the south.
My Cousins live in the South.
