items.explain: Capitalize a direction word when it names a region ('the South'), and keep common nouns like 'cousins' lowercase.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
items.explain: Seasons are normally lowercase, but 'Winter' gets a capital here only because it starts the sentence — and 'December' is always capitalized.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: The menu features Italian pasta and Greek salad.
The menu features italian pasta and greek salad.
The menu features Italian pasta and greek salad.
items.explain: Adjectives made from country names (Italian, Greek) keep their capitals even when describing everyday foods.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: We read "The Gift of the Magi" in class.
We read "The Gift Of The Magi" in class.
We read "the gift of the magi" in class.
items.explain: In titles, capitalize the first word and all major words, but keep little words like 'of' and 'the' lowercase mid-title.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: I asked Mom if my grandma could come.
I asked mom if my grandma could come.
I asked Mom if my Grandma could come.
items.explain: Capitalize a family word when it stands in for a name ('Mom'), but lowercase it after a possessive like 'my grandma.'

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
items.explain: Holidays like Thanksgiving are proper nouns, but the bird 'turkey' stays lowercase — only the country Turkey gets a capital.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: He typed the essay on his Dell laptop.
He typed the essay on his dell laptop.
He typed the essay on his Dell Laptop.
items.explain: Brand names like Dell are capitalized, but the ordinary product word 'laptop' is not.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
items.explain: Acronyms like FBI are written in ALL capital letters — never just the first one.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: Can Dad drive us to practice?
Can dad drive us to practice?
Can Dad drive us to Practice?
items.explain: 'Dad' is capitalized when it stands in for his name, but 'practice' is a common noun and stays lowercase.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: My dad works with his father downtown.
My Dad works with his father downtown.
my dad works with his Father downtown.
items.explain: After a possessive like 'my' or 'his,' family words are common nouns and stay lowercase.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: The probe left Earth and reached Mars.
The probe left earth and reached Mars.
The probe left Earth and reached mars.
items.explain: Both Earth and Mars are planet names here, so both are capitalized as proper nouns.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: He knelt and dug in the earth.
He knelt and dug in the Earth.
he knelt and dug in the earth.
items.explain: When 'earth' means soil or dirt rather than the planet, it stays lowercase.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: The dog slept in the warm sun.
The dog slept in the warm Sun.
the dog slept in the warm sun.
items.explain: 'Sun' meaning everyday sunshine is a common noun and stays lowercase, and every sentence starts with a capital.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: He takes History 101 and enjoys math.
He takes history 101 and enjoys math.
He takes History 101 and enjoys Math.
items.explain: A specific course title like History 101 is capitalized, but a general subject like math is not.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
items.explain: Named historical periods like the Renaissance are proper nouns, and country names always take capitals.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: He wrote a report on the Civil War.
He wrote a report on the civil war.
He wrote a report on the Civil war.
items.explain: A named historical event capitalizes every word of its name — both 'Civil' and 'War.'

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: My favorite book is Charlotte's Web.
My favorite book is Charlotte's web.
My favorite book is charlotte's Web.
items.explain: Capitalize every major word in a book title — 'Web' is part of the title, not an ordinary noun.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: Many Italian-American families live in Boston.
Many Italian-american families live in Boston.
Many italian-American families live in Boston.
items.explain: In a hyphenated proper noun, BOTH halves keep their capitals — Italian and American are each proper adjectives.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: He studies English and chemistry at school.
He studies english and chemistry at school.
He studies English and Chemistry at school.
items.explain: School subjects are lowercase EXCEPT languages — English comes from a country name, chemistry does not.

items.prompt: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: We stayed up late on New Year's Eve.
We stayed up late on new year's eve.
We stayed up late on New Year's eve.
items.explain: Capitalize every word of a holiday's full name — 'Eve' is part of the name New Year's Eve.

drills.title: Spot the Error
drills.blurb: Find the one part that's wrong.

items.prompt: The list of chores were posted on the fridge.
items.explain: The subject is the singular "list," so it should be "was posted," not "were posted."

items.prompt: My brother and me built a fort in the backyard.
items.explain: As part of the subject it should be "and I" — test it alone: "I built a fort," not "me built."

items.prompt: He sings really good at every recital.
items.explain: "Good" is an adjective; to describe how he sings, use the adverb "well."

items.prompt: The robot lowered it's arm and beeped twice.
items.explain: "It's" means "it is" — the possessive is "its," with no apostrophe.

items.prompt: We couldn't hardly see the trail in the fog.
items.explain: "Hardly" is already negative, so "couldn't hardly" doubles up — say "could hardly."

items.prompt: Yesterday, Marco walks to the market and bought fresh bread.
items.explain: "Yesterday" and "bought" set the past tense, so "walks" should be "walked."

items.prompt: The movie was different than the book in every way.
items.explain: The standard pairing is "different from," not "different than."

items.prompt: Neither of the answers seems right to me.
items.explain: No error — "neither" is singular, so the singular "seems" is exactly right.

items.prompt: Of the two routes, the coastal road is the most scenic.
items.explain: Comparing only two things takes the comparative "more scenic" — save "most" for three or more.

items.prompt: The coach gave the trophy to Sara and I.
items.explain: After the preposition "to" you need the object form: "Sara and me" ("to me," never "to I").

items.prompt: The dog waited patient by the door all afternoon.
items.explain: To describe how the dog waited, use the adverb "patiently," not the adjective "patient."

items.prompt: Each of the hikers carries a whistle for emergencies.
items.explain: No error — "each" is singular, so the singular "carries" agrees perfectly.

items.prompt: By noon, the bakers had went through every bag of flour.
items.explain: After "had" use the past participle: "had gone," not "had went."

items.prompt: This puzzle is more harder than the last one.
items.explain: "Harder" is already comparative — adding "more" doubles it, so drop the "more."

items.prompt: The pack of wolves howl at the moon each night.
items.explain: The subject is the singular "pack," so it should be "howls," not "howl."

items.prompt: There were less students in class after the holiday.
items.explain: Students can be counted, so use "fewer students" — save "less" for amounts you can't count.

items.prompt: He has ran three marathons since April.
items.explain: After "has" use the past participle: "has run," not "has ran."

items.prompt: The scouts didn't find nothing in the old cave.
items.explain: "Didn't" and "nothing" make a double negative — say "didn't find anything."

items.prompt: The geese fly south when the weather turns cold.
items.explain: No error — plural "geese fly" and singular "weather turns" both agree perfectly.

items.prompt: First we set up the tents, than we gathered firewood.
items.explain: For a sequence in time use "then" — "than" is only for comparisons.

items.prompt: Between you and I, the sequel was disappointing.
items.explain: After the preposition "between" you need the object form: "between you and me."

items.prompt: The results were consistent to our earlier findings.
items.explain: The standard pairing is "consistent with," not "consistent to."

items.prompt: Every student must bring their permission slip on Friday.
items.explain: "Every student" is singular, so the pronoun should match: "his permission slip," not "their."

items.prompt: Both cat's were asleep on the windowsill.
items.explain: A plain plural takes no apostrophe — it should be "Both cats were asleep."

items.prompt: The committee has posted its decision on the door.
items.explain: No error — the collective "committee" is singular, so "has" and "its" both fit.

items.prompt: The lake had froze solid by the middle of January.
items.explain: After "had" use the past participle: "had frozen," not "had froze."

items.prompt: The cheetah runs faster than any animal on the savanna.
items.explain: The cheetah is itself an animal, so it must run faster than "any other animal."

items.prompt: The prize goes to whoever finishes first.
items.explain: No error — "whoever" is the subject of "finishes," so the subject form is right even after "to."

items.prompt: Us volunteers stacked the chairs after the assembly.
items.explain: The subject needs the subject form: "We volunteers stacked" — test it alone: "We stacked," not "Us stacked."

items.prompt: The quality of his essays have improved this term.
items.explain: The subject is the singular "quality," not "essays," so it should be "has improved."

items.prompt: Because the ferry left early.
items.explain: "Because" starts a dependent clause that never gets finished — that's a fragment.

items.prompt: Close the door quietly.
items.explain: Commands are complete sentences — the subject "you" is understood.

items.prompt: I love astronomy it makes the night sky feel like a story.
items.explain: Two independent clauses are fused with no punctuation or conjunction — a classic run-on.

items.prompt: After the rain stopped, we hiked to the ridge.
items.explain: A dependent clause plus a full independent clause makes a complete sentence.

items.prompt: A drawer full of mismatched socks and old batteries.
items.explain: There's a subject but no main verb — nothing ever happens, so it's a fragment.

items.prompt: The tide came in fast, we grabbed our towels and ran.
items.explain: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses — this comma splice is a run-on.

items.prompt: Hoping to catch the last train home.
items.explain: An "-ing" phrase with no subject or main verb is a fragment — who was hoping?

items.prompt: The kettle whistled, and everyone gathered in the kitchen.
items.explain: A comma plus the conjunction "and" joins the two clauses correctly — complete sentence.

items.prompt: He opened the letter, then he read it aloud twice.
items.explain: "Then" isn't a conjunction, so the comma splices two independent clauses — a run-on.

items.prompt: While the bread was still warm from the oven.
items.explain: "While" makes this a dependent clause left hanging — it needs a main clause.

items.prompt: Although he was tired, he finished the mural.
items.explain: The "although" clause attaches to a full independent clause, so the sentence is complete.

items.prompt: The recipe looked simple, however it took us three hours.
items.explain: "However" can't glue clauses with just a comma — use a semicolon or a new sentence.

items.prompt: Which is exactly why we brought umbrellas.
items.explain: A "which" clause standing alone is a fragment — it must lean on a main sentence.

items.prompt: Unless the votes are counted by midnight.
items.explain: This is a lone dependent clause starting with "unless" and never delivers the independent clause it promises.

items.prompt: Hand me the smallest wrench in the drawer.
items.explain: An imperative has an understood subject "you," so this is one complete independent clause.

items.prompt: The alarm rang nobody moved.
items.explain: Two independent clauses ("the alarm rang" and "nobody moved") are fused together with no punctuation or conjunction.

items.prompt: A gifted violinist with a fear of stages.
items.explain: This is a verbless noun phrase, an appositive left standing alone with no subject-verb core.

items.prompt: He fixed the antenna, the signal came back instantly.
items.explain: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses, so this is a comma splice.

items.prompt: Whenever the fog rolls in, the harbor bells ring twice.
items.explain: A dependent clause correctly attached to the independent clause "the harbor bells ring twice" makes a complete complex sentence.

items.prompt: Stunned by the sudden roar of the crowd.
items.explain: This -ed participial phrase has no subject or main verb, so it cannot stand alone.

items.prompt: The museum was free on Sundays, we went every week.
items.explain: Two independent clauses are spliced together with only a comma, which makes a run-on.

items.prompt: The violinist who lost his sheet music improvised the entire second movement.
items.explain: The relative clause "who lost his sheet music" is embedded inside one complete independent clause with subject "violinist" and verb "improvised."

items.prompt: Sprinting the length of the pier against the wind.
items.explain: An -ing phrase by itself has no subject and no finite verb, so it is a fragment.

items.prompt: The bridge was icy, therefore the buses took the long route.
items.explain: A conjunctive adverb like "therefore" needs a semicolon or a period before it, so a comma here creates a run-on.

items.prompt: The power failed; the backup generators hummed to life.
items.explain: A semicolon legally joins two closely related independent clauses, so this is a correctly punctuated complete sentence.

items.prompt: Who taught himself to juggle in a single weekend.
items.explain: This stranded relative clause describes someone but never attaches to an independent clause.

items.prompt: He studied all night the exam still surprised him.
items.explain: "He studied all night" and "the exam still surprised him" are two independent clauses fused with nothing between them.

items.prompt: The old surveyor with the battered brass compass and the leaky boots finally reached the fire tower at dusk.
items.explain: Despite its length, this is one independent clause with a single subject "surveyor" and a single main verb "reached."

items.prompt: The cake was baked by my grandmother.
items.explain: The subject "cake" receives the action — "was baked by…" is the passive pattern.

items.prompt: The dog chased the mail truck down the street.
items.explain: The subject "dog" performs the chasing, so the sentence is active.

items.prompt: The bridge was painted last summer.
items.explain: Even without a "by" phrase, "was painted" shows the subject receiving the action — passive.

items.prompt: Maria planted tulips along the fence.
items.explain: Maria does the planting — subject acts, so it's active voice.

items.prompt: The chef tasted the soup before serving it.
items.explain: The subject "chef" performs the action "tasted" — that's active.

items.prompt: The missing keys were found under the couch.
items.explain: "Were found" is be + past participle, and the keys receive the action — passive.

items.prompt: The storm knocked out power across the valley.
items.explain: The storm does the knocking out — the subject acts, so it's active.

items.prompt: The anthem is sung before every game.
items.explain: "Is sung" = be + past participle, and the anthem doesn't sing itself — passive.

items.prompt: The committee has approved the new mural.
items.explain: "Has approved" is a perfect tense, not be + participle — the committee acts, so it's active.

items.prompt: Our tent had been flattened by the wind overnight.
items.explain: "Had been flattened by…" shows the tent receiving the action — passive voice.

items.prompt: The winners will be announced at noon.
items.explain: "Will be announced" is future passive — the winners receive the announcing.

items.prompt: The students were reading quietly in the library.
items.explain: "Were reading" is past progressive, not passive — the students are doing the reading.

items.prompt: Mistakes get made when everyone rushes.
items.explain: "Get made" is the get-passive — the mistakes receive the action of being made.

items.prompt: The janitor swept the gymnasium after the assembly.
items.explain: The subject "janitor" performs the sweeping, so the sentence is active.

items.prompt: The letters were delivered by a drone.
items.explain: The subject "letters" receives the action, with "were delivered" plus a "by" phrase naming the doer.

items.prompt: He carried the groceries up three flights of stairs.
items.explain: The subject "he" does the carrying, so the voice is active.

items.prompt: The windows are washed every Friday.
items.explain: The subject "windows" receives the washing in a be-plus-participle construction, with the doer left unstated.

items.prompt: The interns have completed the safety training.
items.explain: "Have completed" is present perfect active; the subject "interns" did the completing, not received it.

items.prompt: The catcher got hurt sliding into home plate.
items.explain: This is a get-passive: the subject "catcher" receives the hurt rather than inflicting it.

items.prompt: The engineers were testing the turbine all afternoon.
items.explain: "Were testing" is past progressive active; the subject "engineers" performs the testing despite the "were."

items.prompt: He was awarded a medal for bravery.
items.explain: The subject "he" receives the awarding, and "a medal" is a retained object left over from the active version.

items.prompt: The captain seems exhausted after the long voyage.
items.explain: "Seems" is a linking verb and "exhausted" works as an adjective, so this is not a be-plus-participle passive.

items.prompt: The road is being repaved this week.
items.explain: "Is being repaved" is a progressive passive: the subject "road" receives the repaving from an unnamed crew.

items.prompt: The recruits were happy about the early dismissal.
items.explain: "Were happy" is a linking verb plus an adjective, not be plus a past participle, so no action is being received.

items.prompt: The students were given extra time on the exam.
items.explain: The subject "students" receives the giving, and "extra time" is the retained object of this passive.

items.prompt: By Friday, the crew will have poured all the concrete.
items.explain: "Will have poured" is future perfect active; the subject "crew" does the pouring.

items.prompt: Promises were broken during the negotiations.
items.explain: This agentless passive puts the receiver "promises" in the subject slot and quietly omits whoever broke them.

items.prompt: The manuscript had been rejected twice before it found a publisher.
items.explain: "Had been rejected" is past perfect passive: the subject "manuscript" receives the rejecting.
